questions.prompt: What does setting a breakpoint do?
choices: Deletes the line it is on
Pauses the program just before that line runs, with everything still in memory
Prints the value of every variable
questions.explain: The value of a breakpoint is the pause, not the stop. The program is frozen mid-run with its variables intact, so you can ask questions you had not thought of in advance.

questions.prompt: Match each debugger control to what it does.
right: Run to the end of the current function and stop after it returns
Run the next line, going inside any function it calls
Run the next line without descending into the functions it calls
questions.explain: Step over and step into differ only on whether you follow a call. Choosing the wrong one is how people end up several frames deep inside a library they did not mean to read.

questions.prompt: What can a debugger do that a print statement cannot?
choices: Show the value of a variable
Let you inspect anything at all once stopped, without deciding in advance what mattered
questions.explain: A print commits you to a guess about which variable is interesting. Stopped in a debugger you can look at all of them, including the one you had no reason to suspect.

questions.prompt: When is reaching for the debugger a better first move than adding prints?
choices: The bug is deep inside a chain of calls
You do not yet know which variable is wrong
The program is slow to restart, so each print costs a full re-run
You already know exactly which line to look at
questions.explain: The debugger earns its setup cost when you cannot yet name the question. If you already know the line and the variable, one print is faster than starting a session.

reflection-exercise1.hint: A breakpoint pauses rather than stops. Say what you can do during that pause that you could not do otherwise.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Compare the two honestly. A print commits you to a guess in advance; the debugger does not, but costs more to set up.
